props.title: Dead & Buried
props.initialSlug: Small town's dead return as murderous imposters

sections.content: **Dead & Buried** (1981) stands as one of horror's most underappreciated gems, blending small-town paranoia with zombie elements years before **Re-Animator** (1985) hit screens. The film's ingenious twist on the undead subgenre shares DNA with **Invasion of the Body Snatchers** (1978), but adds a unique mortician's touch that predates the forensic fascination of shows like CSI by decades. Director Gary Sherman crafts a genuinely unsettling atmosphere that recalls the best of **The Twilight Zone**, while Stan Winston's early effects work proves why he'd become Hollywood's go-to creature creator.

sections.content: The film's influence echoes through later small-town horror mysteries like **Twin Peaks** (1990) and **In the Mouth of Madness** (1994). Its clever use of a sheriff protagonist investigating his own community predates similar setups in **Hot Fuzz** (2007) and **The Wicker Man** (1973). The mortician character, played brilliantly by Jack Albertson in his final role, established a template for creepy funeral directors that influenced everything from **Pet Sematary** (1989) to **Phantasm** (1979).

What sets **Dead & Buried** apart is its sophisticated approach to horror, eschewing simple scares for psychological dread. The film's exploration of identity and community paranoia shares thematic DNA with **Society** (1989) and **Parents** (1989), while its police procedural elements feel like a horror precursor to **True Detective** (2014). The practical effects, particularly the needle-in-eye scene, remain shocking even by today's standards. SUBHEAD: Small Town Horror Evolution

sections.content: **Dead & Buried** helped establish conventions that would become staples of small-town horror, influencing films like **Salem's Lot** (1979) and **Storm of the Century** (1999). Its blend of police work and supernatural elements created a template followed by **Angel Heart** (1987) and **Fallen** (1998), while its twist ending set a standard for supernatural mysteries that continues through modern films like **The Others** (2001) and **Shutter Island** (2010).
